A hydroelectric dam on the Paraná River, on the border between Brazil and Paraguay, built from the mid 1970s and producing power from 1984. For years it was the largest power plant in the world; China's Three Gorges Dam later passed it in capacity, though Itaipu has at times produced more power in a year.

The two countries agreed on it in the Itaipu Treaty of 1973, under military governments on both sides, and own it equally. Its name, from Guarani, refers to an island at the site. The dam flooded the Guaíra Falls, among the largest waterfalls in the world by volume, which were dynamited. Tens of thousands of people, including Guarani communities, were moved.

Itaipu supplies a large share of Brazil's electricity and almost all of Paraguay's. Paraguay sold most of its half to Brazil at a fixed price, a long running grievance that was renegotiated in 2009. Like the Aswan High Dam, it is a symbol of 20th century faith in huge engineering.
